html:
The Saka were Iranian-speaking nomads of the Central Asian steppes, the eastern cousins of the Scythians. The map places them around 100 BCE in the lands of the Syr Darya, Ferghana and the Tian Shan, in what is now Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan.

They were horse riders and herders, buried their chiefs in large mounds and made fine gold work, such as the Golden Man of Issyk. Persian kings fought and recruited them.

In the second century BCE the Yuezhi, fleeing the Xiongnu, pushed the Saka from their pastures. Many Saka moved south into Bactria, then into eastern Iran, which became Sakastan, and fought the Parthian Empire. Others went on into northwest India, where their kings are known as the Indo-Scythians. Saka rulers, the Western Satraps, held western India until about 400 CE.
